did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ziba brought David two saddled donkeys, loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, one hundred bunches of raisins, one hundred summer fruits, and a wineskin—a provision for the king and his people during their flight through the wilderness.

Did you know? Ziba claimed that Mephibosheth had remained in Jerusalem because he hoped that the house of Israel would restore his grandfather Saul’s kingdom to him. The chapter reports Ziba’s claim but does not independently confirm it.

Did you know? Based on Ziba’s report, David gave him all of Mephibosheth’s property. The chapter presents this decision as having been made on the basis of a single report; later in the story, David revisits the dispute between Ziba and Mephibosheth.
Did you know? Shimei son of Gera, who belonged to the house of Saul, came out from Bahurim to meet David and cursed him while David was fleeing from Jerusalem.
Did you know? Abishai son of Zeruiah asked David to kill Shimei for his curses, but David rejected his proposal and would not allow anyone to harm him.

Did you know? David explained that if his own son was seeking his life, how much more should Shimei the Benjaminite be allowed to curse him. In this way, David chose restraint and acceptance of suffering instead of immediate revenge.
Did you know? David did not regard Shimei’s curse as merely a personal insult. He said that perhaps the Lord would see his affliction and repay him with good instead of the curse.

Did you know? Hushai the Archite, who is called David’s friend in the chapter, greeted Absalom by saying, “Long live the king!” even though he had earlier declared his loyalty to David. Through his words, he managed to remain close to Absalom.

Did you know? Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in to David’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. According to the explanation given in the chapter, this act was meant to demonstrate that the kingdom had passed from David to Absalom and to strengthen the hands of the supporters of the rebellion.

Did you know? Ahithophel’s advice was regarded as highly authoritative in those days. The text compares its value to inquiring of the word of God and emphasizes that it was considered valid both by David and by Absalom.
